The Peck Deck
Field Handbook

A bird feeder that watches itself: a Raspberry Pi sees a visitor, photographs it, names the species, and tells you about it — end to end, on your own hardware, on your own network.

Revision25 July 2026 · main
CoversMilestones M1–M6 · FLEDGE Phases 0–8
AudienceFeeder owners & contributors
Source of truthPRD.md · CLAUDE.md · FLEDGE_ROADMAP.md

This handbook is two documents sharing one spine. Part I is the owner's manual — what the thing does, how to put one in your backyard, and what every screen of the web app means. It assumes nothing but a willingness to follow instructions. Part II is the engineering guide — architecture, data model, API surface, the machine-learning tiers, and the reasoning behind decisions that would otherwise look arbitrary. Read the part you need; the other one is there when you want it.

Sightings recorded141in the reference database
Species catalogued13of 965 the model knows
Automated tests420backend + frontend + integration
API operations36across 27 paths
Tier 1 latency57.9mson the Pi 5 itself
How to read the badges Sections carry an audience tag. Owner means you never need to open a terminal. Engineer means you will. Where a topic matters to both — notifications, the classification tiers — it appears in both parts at different depths rather than being written once at the wrong altitude.

1 · What Peck Deck is Owner

Peck Deck is a bird feeder with a camera and a brain. When a bird lands, the feeder notices, takes a photograph, works out what species it is, and files the result. A few seconds later your phone buzzes: Black-capped Chickadee at Backyard Maple, 94% confident, sighting #24.

Everything lives in your house. The photographs go into a database on your own computer, not somebody's cloud. The species identification runs on the feeder itself, so it keeps working when the internet does not. Nothing is subscription- gated and there is no account with a company in it.

The two halves

A Peck Deck installation is always two pieces of equipment in two places.

PieceWhat it does
The feeder unit
Outside, on a pole or under an eave		 A Raspberry Pi 5 with a camera, a sensor that tells it a bird has arrived, and a battery. It photographs, identifies, and uploads. It has a local memory so an outage loses nothing.
The home computer
Indoors, always on		 Stores every sighting and photograph, serves the web app you browse, sends the notifications, and — if it has a suitable graphics card — offers a second, more accurate opinion on hard identifications.

What it is not

  • It is not a security camera. There is no live video stream. It captures a still photograph on each visit; video is designed for but not built.
  • It is not reachable from the internet. By design, the web app is served on your home network only. That is a deliberate safety decision, not a missing feature.
  • It does not listen. There is no microphone and no audio-based detection.
  • It does not manage a fleet. One household, several feeders — that works. A hundred feeders across a county does not.
Honest status, July 2026 The software is finished and tested; the physical feeder is not. The camera, identification, upload, database, notifications and web app all work and have been run on real hardware. What is missing is a trigger sensor wired to the Pi and one full outdoor field test with a real bird. §19 is a complete build guide, and it is honest about which parts are proven on a bench and which are still on paper.

2 · What you're actually getting Owner

Hardware, roughly $500 all in

Nothing here is custom-manufactured. Every part is off-the-shelf and orderable today. The two columns separate what the project has verified from what it has only specified.

PartApprox.StatusNote
Raspberry Pi 5, 8 GB$80VerifiedThe feeder's computer. 4× Cortex-A76.
Camera Module 3 Wide (IMX708)$35Verified~300 KB JPEG at 1920×1080 in about a second.
SD card, 64 GB$12VerifiedOS, models, and the local photo cache.
Perch microswitch (SPDT roller lever)$8/10pkSpecifiedThe trigger. See §19.3 for why this and not a motion sensor.
USB-C PD power bank, 25,000 mAh$50Specified~20 hours continuous, ~2 days with dawn/dusk scheduling.
IP65 enclosure + vent + desiccant$60SpecifiedThe vent is not optional. §19.4.
Pole, baffle, conduit, gland kit$85SpecifiedSquirrels are a cabling problem, not a bird problem.
Home computerhave oneVerifiedAny machine that can run Docker. A gaming GPU unlocks Tier 2 but is optional.

Software, all included

The whole stack starts with one command and needs no licences.

Web app
Dashboard, photo gallery, species library, station settings, user management. Installs to a phone home screen and works offline.
Species identification
Three independent identifiers of increasing power. The first runs on the feeder with no network at all.
Notifications
Email, text message, and browser push. Each person chooses their own channels.
History & export
Every sighting kept forever, with charts, and downloadable as CSV or JSON.
Backups
One script. Because the photographs live inside the database, the database backup is the photo backup.

What a sighting costs you

A single visit produces roughly 300 KB — one JPEG plus a row of metadata. A busy feeder in winter might log 150 visits a day.

3 · Setting one up Owner

Two installations, in this order: the home computer first, because the feeder needs somewhere to send things.

3.1 · The home computer

You need Docker Desktop. Everything else is fetched automatically.

  1. Get the code 
    git clone https://github.com/dnorris823/Peck_Deck.git
cd Peck_Deck
  2. Create your settings file

    Copy the example and open it in any text editor.

    cp .env.example .env

    Change two things. Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD to anything you like, and replace JWT_SECRET with a long random string — this one signs your login sessions, so it should not stay at the shipped default:

    python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))"
  3. Start it 
    docker compose up --build

    The first run takes a few minutes. When it settles, both containers report healthy — the database schema has been created and the API can actually serve.

  4. Check it's alive

    Visit http://localhost:8000/ready in a browser. You want:

    {"status": "ready", "database": "ok",
 "migrations": "ok", "applied_revision": "233452d81bee"}
  5. Start the web app 
    cd frontend
npm ci
npm run build && npm run preview

    Open http://localhost:4173. Use npm run build && npm run preview rather than npm run dev — the offline support and phone install only activate in a real build.

  6. Take a look before you have hardware

    You do not need a feeder to see the app working. A simulator drives the real upload path with invented birds:

    # two weeks of history, then exit
python -m backend.simulator --mode burst --count 120 --days 14

# or a live drip — watch the dashboard update
python -m backend.simulator --mode live --interval 8
Leave it running The home computer should stay on. If it sleeps, the feeder cannot deliver and will queue sightings locally until it wakes — nothing is lost, but notifications arrive late and the dashboard goes quiet. On Windows, set the machine's sleep timer to Never while plugged in.

3.2 · The feeder

The full physical build — enclosure, power, mounting, weatherproofing — is §19. This is the software side, which you do at a desk before anything goes outside.

  1. Prepare the Pi

    Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit). Enable the camera in raspi-config under Interface Options. Then, from the project folder:

    sudo apt install -y python3-pip python3-venv python3-picamera2
python3 -m venv --system-site-packages .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r raspberry_pi_code/requirements.txt tflite-runtime

    The --system-site-packages flag matters: the camera library is installed by apt, not pip, and the virtual environment has to be able to see it.

  2. Fetch the identification model 
    python scripts/fetch_models.py

    About 3.5 MB, checksum-verified. The model file is not stored in the repository because it is a third-party binary with its own licence.

  3. Register the feeder with the home computer

    In the web app, go to Devices → Add and give it a name and location. You get back a long device token. This is the feeder's password; copy it.

  4. Point the feeder at home

    Create raspberry_pi_code/.env:

    BACKEND_URL=http://192.168.1.100:8000
DEVICE_TOKEN=<the token from step 3>
TRIGGER_TYPE=ir_beam
TRIGGER_GPIO_PIN=17
CACHE_DIR=/home/pi/peck_deck_cache

    Use your home computer's actual address. TRIGGER_TYPE=ir_beam is correct for the recommended perch switch as well as for a beam — both are falling-edge sensors. §19.3 explains why the shipped default of pir is the wrong choice.

  5. Run it 
    python -m raspberry_pi_code.main

    To start automatically on boot, install the systemd unit given in SETUP.md §9.

The one that will get you If you rebuild the database, every device token issued by the old one stops working. The feeder keeps photographing and keeps queueing, but every upload is refused and nothing appears in the app. This happened during hardware bring-up and took a while to spot, because a refused token used to be reported as "backend unreachable". It is now reported accurately — if the Pi's log says "Device token rejected", re-register the device and paste the new token into .env.

Six screens. Everything is reachable from the left rail, and everything reads like a field naturalist's journal because that is deliberate.

5 · Notifications Owner

Three independent channels. Each person picks their own; nobody's choice affects anybody else's.

ChannelYou'll getSet up in
EmailSpecies, station, confidence, how many times you've seen it, a Wikipedia link, and the photograph inline.Settings → Notifications. Needs a SendGrid key on the server.
TextOne line: Peck Deck: Blue Jay at Backyard Maple — sighting #13. plus a link.Settings → Notifications, and a phone number on your account. Needs Twilio on the server.
Browser pushA phone notification with the app closed. Title, confidence, count and location.Settings → Notifications, on each device you want alerts on. §6.

Why you won't be spammed

A flock of starlings can occupy a perch for an hour. Three separate mechanisms keep that from becoming an hour of buzzing.

Debounce
On the feeder. One capture per visit, default 30 seconds. A bird that lands three times in a minute is one sighting.
Quiet interval
On the server, per person per station. Default 60 seconds. Adjustable in Settings.
New species only
Optional. Alerts you the first time a species appears at a station and never again. Good for a household member who wants the interesting news only.
Channel toggles
Email and text are switches on your account. Push is per browser — see below.
Notifications never block a sighting If SendGrid is down or your phone has been offline for a week, the sighting is still recorded, the photograph is still stored, and the app still shows it. Delivery failures are logged and dropped. A missed notification is never a lost bird.

6 · Peck Deck on your phone Owner

There is no app store. The web app installs itself.

  1. Open the app in your phone's browser

    Use the home computer's address on your network, e.g. http://192.168.1.100:4173.

  2. Add it to your home screen

    Chrome offers Install app. On iPhone, Share → Add to Home Screen. It then opens without browser chrome, like any other app.

  3. Turn on push, per phone

    Settings → Notifications → enable browser notifications, on that phone. Push permission belongs to the device, not the account — your laptop and your phone are separate opt-ins.

What works with no signal

Open the app in a dead zone and it still paints — your last-loaded sightings, species and stations, from the phone's own storage, with a small You're offline banner. What you cannot do offline is change anything: this is a read cache, not a sync queue. Sign out and it is wiped, because it holds one person's records.

7 · When something goes wrong Owner

SymptomMost likely causeWhat to do
Dashboard is empty and won't load The server isn't running. Visit http://localhost:8000/ready. If it doesn't answer, run docker compose up. If it answers not_ready, the database is starting or a migration is pending — give it a minute.
No new sightings, but the feeder has power Nine times in ten: a stale device token. Check the feeder's log (sudo journalctl -u peck-deck -f). "Device token rejected" means re-register the station and update DEVICE_TOKEN. "Backend unreachable" is genuinely the network.
Sightings arrive in a sudden burst, hours late Nothing is wrong. That's the offline queue draining. The feeder saved everything through the outage and uploaded it when the network returned. Delayed sightings are marked as such.
Every identification is confident and wrong A model / taxonomy mismatch. The most dangerous failure this system has, because everything else looks fine. Run python scripts/validate_tier1.py — a misaligned taxonomy scores near zero. Never hand-edit taxonomy.csv.
Confidence has quietly collapsed Physical, not software. Dirty or fogged lens; camera knocked out of aim; feeder moved so birds perch outside the frame; wildfire smoke. Look at recent photographs — the answer is almost always visible in them.
No email or texts Provider keys not set. Email needs SENDGRID_API_KEY; texts need the three TWILIO_* values in .env. Restart the server after editing. Nothing is queued for later — unsent is unsent.
Push worked, then silently stopped The server's push keypair changed. Browsers bake the public key into their subscription. Rotating VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY invalidates every existing one. Re-subscribe on each device — and don't rotate it again.
Cloud identification returns "unavailable" The API key isn't set — or is set under the wrong name. The code reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. .env.example mistakenly suggests CLAUDE_API_KEY, which does nothing. See Appendix C.
Feeder gets hot / stops in a heatwave Thermal throttling. The Pi 5 throttles above about 80 °C and has been seen doing so on a bench in open air. A sealed box in July needs the mitigations in §19.4.
The two commands worth knowing 
# is the server healthy?
curl http://localhost:8000/ready

# what is the feeder actually doing?
sudo journalctl -u peck-deck -f

8 · Architecture Engineer

Four deployable units, three of which run on one machine. They are separated by where they must physically run, not by taste: the Pi code must run without the backend, the inference server must have the GPU, and the API must have the database.

8.1 · Repository layout

Peck_Deck/
├── raspberry_pi_code/    # feeder runtime — self-contained, HTTP-only
│   ├── trigger/          #   PIR + IR-beam GPIO edge sources
│   ├── camera/           #   picamera2 wrapper + a headless stub
│   ├── classification/   #   tier1 tflite · tier2 gpu · tier3 cloud
│   ├── storage/          #   rolling image cache + offline queue
│   └── pipeline.py       #   trigger → capture → classify → upload
├── backend/              # Litestar REST API (Docker)
│   ├── auth/ users/ devices/ species/ sightings/ stats/
│   ├── notifications/    #   email · sms · web push · wikipedia
│   ├── classification/   #   Tier 3 Claude relay
│   ├── migrations/       #   Alembic — owns the schema
│   ├── simulator.py      #   virtual feeder driving the real Pi client
│   └── demo.py           #   read-only demo middleware + boot seed
├── inference_server/     # FastAPI + torch, bare metal, RTX 5080
├── frontend/             # React + Vite, installable PWA
├── machine_learning/     # taxonomy CSVs; weights are fetched, not committed
├── integration_tests/    # real Postgres + live in-process servers
└── scripts/              # migrate · backup · restore · fetch_models · …
The framework trap The backend is Litestar. The inference server is FastAPI. They are different services with different idioms, and mixing them up is the single most common mistake when working in this repo. Litestar's controllers, guards and Provide dependency injection look superficially like FastAPI's and behave differently.

8.2 · The life of a sighting

This is the path everything else exists to serve. Read it once and most of the codebase becomes predictable.

  1. Edge on a GPIO pin

    trigger/ registers an interrupt with bouncetime=200 and pushes to an asyncio.Queue. PIRTrigger is rising-edge with a pull-down; IRBeamTrigger is falling-edge with a pull-up.

  2. Debounce, then capture

    Pipeline.handle_trigger takes a lock and checks debounce_seconds against a monotonic clock. A trigger arriving during a capture is dropped, not queued — a second photograph of the same visit is not worth the battery.

  3. Classify down the tier chain

    _classify walks the tiers in preference order. A tier that fails is skipped; a tier that answers below the confidence threshold is also skipped, but its answer is retained. §12.

  4. Upload — one multipart POST

    Image bytes and metadata go together to POST /sightings. There is no separate upload-then-register step, so there is no window in which a photograph exists without a record.

  5. Or queue it

    The outcome is typed. Only OK clears; RETRY queues; UNAUTHORIZED queues and shouts; REJECTED drops, because replaying a malformed request forever only poisons the queue.

  6. Server side: resolve, store, enrich, notify

    The controller finds-or-creates the Species row, writes the Sighting with the JPEG as bytea, and fires two asyncio.create_task calls — species enrichment and notification dispatch — neither of which the response waits on.

8.3 · Design decisions worth knowing

DecisionRationale
Images in Postgres as bytea Media and metadata can never disagree, and one pg_dump is a complete backup. The cost is real — you can't serve images from a CDN and rows are fat — but for a single household it buys a category of bug that simply cannot occur.
Single multipart upload Two-step upload has a failure window that leaves orphaned media. One POST is atomic per sighting.
Pi code depends on nothing in backend/ It talks HTTP only. The feeder can be updated, run, and tested with the server absent — which is also what makes the contract tests meaningful.
Typed upload outcomes A boolean collapsed "network down" and "token refused" into one answer, so the pipeline retried a permanently-refused sighting forever while logging the wrong cause. __bool__ keeps every if ok: call site working.
Alembic owns the schema create_all() only ever creates missing tables, so every model change after the first deploy silently never reached the database.
Fire-and-forget notifications The Pi's upload must not wait on SendGrid. The service opens its own session, so the request's session lifetime is irrelevant.
Two auth schemes, strictly separated A device token is not accepted on user routes and a user JWT is not accepted on device routes. Separate guards, no shared fallback.

9 · The four services Engineer

9.1 · Pi runtime — raspberry_pi_code/

Python 3.11, asyncio, ~1,600 lines. Four swappable abstractions behind Pipeline.

trigger/
TriggerBase → PIRTrigger, IRBeamTrigger. Each configures the pull direction and edge that suits its sensor and yields events through an async queue. On a Pi 5 the RP1 chip means RPi.GPIO must resolve to the rpi-lgpio shim; stock RPi.GPIO fails at runtime.
camera/
PiCamera wraps picamera2 as an async context manager. Off-Pi it degrades to a stub so the pipeline is testable anywhere. No autofocus configuration exists yet — see Appendix C.
classification/
Three ClassifierBase implementations returning a common ClassificationResult(common_name, scientific_name, confidence, tier_used).
storage/
LocalCache — the rolling image cache and the JSON-backed offline queue.
api_client.py
BackendClient — aiohttp, multipart upload, UploadOutcome, and a cheap /health reachability probe.

The cache/queue interaction

This deserves its own diagram because it has produced three separate defects, two of which only appeared on real hardware.

Why it is built this way Eviction originally trimmed by mtime with no knowledge of queue.json, so any backlog deeper than 25 destroyed its own oldest entries — the outages long enough to matter were exactly the ones that lost data. Fixing that created a second bug: with queued images protected, the capture currently being classified became the only eviction candidate and was deleted out from under Tier 1 mid-read. Unit tests missed it; the live run did not. Hence evict_if_needed(protect=…).

Tier preference

# pipeline.py — order is the whole policy
"local" → [tier1]
"gpu"   → [tier2, tier1]
"cloud" → [tier3, tier2, tier1]
"auto"  → [tier1, tier2, tier3]   # default: cheapest first

9.2 · Backend API — backend/

Litestar on Python 3.11+, ~8,600 lines including tests. Async throughout: SQLAlchemy 2.0 with asyncpg, aiohttp for outbound calls.

Each domain is a package of four files, and the split is load-bearing:

controller.py
Route handlers, guards, HTTP concerns. No SQL.
operations.py
Database queries. No HTTP. This is what the tests mostly drive.
schemas.py
Request/response dataclasses — the shape the OpenAPI document is generated from.
__init__.py
Package marker.

Cross-cutting modules:

ModuleResponsibility
main.pyApp assembly, CORS, OpenAPI config, startup/shutdown, production boot check.
errors.pyEvery failure serialises to {status_code, type, detail, request_id, extra?}. detail is retained for frontend compatibility. Preserves exc.headers — dropping it once swallowed Retry-After and WWW-Authenticate.
observability.pyRequest-id middleware and a request-id-aware log formatter. Mounted outermost, so even a demo-mode 403 gets an id and an access-log line.
readiness.pyDatabase connectivity and Alembic revision check for /ready.
auth/jwt_utils (bcrypt + HS256), guards (user_guard, owner_guard, device_guard), rate_limit (per-account and per-IP login throttling).
demo.pyASGI middleware enforcing read-only demo mode, plus the boot seed. §14.

9.3 · Inference server — inference_server/

FastAPI + PyTorch + timm, ~370 lines, deliberately small. Runs bare metal, not in Docker, because it needs direct GPU access.

# from the PROJECT ROOT, not inference_server/
pip install -r inference_server/requirements.txt
# RTX 5080 is Blackwell (sm_120) — cu124 has no kernels for it and will fail
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
python -m inference_server

Two endpoints: GET /health (reports model_ready) and POST /classify (multipart image → prediction). The model is loaded once at lifespan startup and cached — which means changing the model requires a restart, a fact that has cost debugging time before.

9.4 · Frontend — frontend/

React 18 + Vite 8, ~6,900 lines. No router and no state library: a route string in App.jsx, and one DataContext holding everything loadAll() fetched. For six screens over one dataset that is the right amount of machinery.

FileRole
App.jsxAuth gate, shell, route switch, live-alert toast.
DataContext.jsxOne fetch of everything; loading / error / stale state.
data.jsfetchRaw + mapAll, split so the offline cache and the live path share one mapper. Storing mapped objects would hand a JSON round trip datetime as a string; a second mapper would drift.
api.jsfetch wrapper: token handling, error envelope unwrapping, 401 → sign-out.
offline.jsLast raw payloads in localStorage. Reads only. Cleared on sign-out and on an expired session.
Charts.jsxHand-rolled SVG charts — no charting library. Crosshair, per-mark tooltips, keyboard focus parity, and a table view on every chart.
SightingImage.jsxIntersectionObserver + authed blob fetch. loading="lazy" can't work here: the image route needs a JWT and an <img src> carries no headers.
BirdPlate.jsxGenerates the stylised species plates from palette + silhouette.
Appearance.jsxPaper / Dusk theme via a data-theme attribute and a token remap.

10 · Data model Engineer

Tables that need explanation

TableNotes
sightings image_data/video_data are bytea. delayed flags an offline-sync upload so the app and the notification can say so. classification_tier_used is a free string, recorded per row rather than inherited from the device — a station set to Auto produces a mix.
species Created on demand at first sighting; the table is empty on a fresh install. Unique on (common_name, genus, species_name). wiki_url, description and family are enriched asynchronously and only fill empty columns, so curated values survive. palette/silhouette/note drive the SVG plates.
devices token is unique and is the feeder's whole credential. battery, signal and last_seen are nullable telemetry from the heartbeat — a freshly registered device has never checked in.
user_preferences One row per user, created lazily on first read or write. Holds quiet_interval_seconds, notify_new_species_only, default_tier, escalation_threshold, debounce_seconds.
push_subscriptions endpoint is unique: re-subscribing must replace the row, not add one that delivers every alert twice. p256dh and auth are the browser's RFC 8291 keys.
Schema changes Change a model → generate a migration. integration_tests/test_migrations.py fails CI if the two drift. The unit suites still build their schema with create_all() for speed; that drift test is the only thing keeping it honest. 
bash scripts/migrate.sh revision --autogenerate -m "add foo"
bash scripts/migrate.sh check   # fail if models drifted

11 · The HTTP API Engineer

27 paths, 36 operations. The generated document is the contract — the table below is a map, not a specification.

After changing a route 
python scripts/export_openapi.py
so the contract change shows up as a diff in review rather than silently.

11.1 · Authentication

Both schemes are Authorization: Bearer <token>, and that is where the similarity ends.

SchemeIssued byUsed for
UserJWTPOST /login, HS256, 24 hEverything the web app does. Carries user_id and role (owner | viewer).
DeviceTokenDevice registration, long-livedPOST /sightings, POST /classify, POST /devices/{id}/heartbeat. Nothing else.

POST/classifydeviceTier 3 relay to Claude. 503 with no key configured.
GET/healthpublicLiveness. Touches nothing.
GET/readypublicReadiness. DB + migration state. 503 when not.
GET/metapublicDemo mode + environment, pre-login.

11.3 · Error envelope

{
  "status_code": 403,
  "type": "Forbidden",
  "detail": "This is a read-only demo instance…",
  "request_id": "3f9c1a2e-…",
  "extra": { "demo_mode": true }
}

Uniform across every controller. request_id ties a user-visible failure to a log line, which is the point of having it.

12 · Classification & machine learning Engineer

Three identifiers of increasing cost and capability, and a fallback policy connecting them.

This was broken until hardware caught it _classify originally advanced only when a tier returned None, so a 0.05-confidence Tier 1 answer won outright and Tiers 2 and 3 were never consulted. config.confidence_threshold was read by no code at all. It took a live Pi to notice.

12.1 · The tiers

TierModelRuns onClassesMeasured
1 LocalGoogle AIY birds_V1
MobileNetV2 / iNaturalist		Pi 5 CPU964 + background20/20 top-1, 57.9 ms, 12 ms load
2 LAN GPUViT-L/14 CLIP fine-tuned on iNat21
timm/vit_large_patch14_clip_336…		RTX 508010,000 → 869 mapped20/20 top-1, 29.1 ms, ~26 s cold load
3 CloudClaude multimodal APIAnthropic, relayedopen vocabularycontract-tested; not benchmarked
20/20 is an upper bound, not an accuracy claim The ground-truth set is 20 Wikipedia lead images: clean, centred, well-lit, frame-filling birds. A feeder camera sees motion blur, bad angles, backlighting and partial occlusion. This measurement proves the model and taxonomy are wired up correctly. It does not tell you the field accuracy, and nobody has that number yet — obtaining it is Stage 1 of §19.6, and it may be the most important unknown in the project.

12.2 · The shared label space

The reason a Tier 1 and a Tier 2 answer are directly comparable is that both resolve to the same 965-row table.

taxonomy.csv is a contract, not a list tier1_tflite.py does self._taxa[argmax]. A row inserted in the wrong place mislabels every sighting while remaining entirely plausible — and shapes, latency, and load all still pass. Regenerate it with build_taxonomy.py; never hand-edit it; run validate_tier1.py after any model change, because a misaligned taxonomy scores near zero there and exits non-zero. That is the only cheap way to catch it.

Two CSVs, not interchangeable

FileRowsWhat it is
taxonomy.csv965The model's label space. Generated. Row order is the index contract.
feeder_species.csv20A curated North American backyard subset. Hand-maintained. Drives the simulator and demo.

The second exists because the simulator's species_weights() makes index 0 the commonest feeder bird. Drawing from all 964 would have handed "most frequent visitor" to whatever sits at index 0 and filled the dashboard with limpkins and cranes.

12.3 · Three details that will bite

Dequantise the output
The TFLite model emits uint8. Without applying the output tensor's scale/zero-point, confidence is a 0–255 integer and the 0.5 threshold is meaningless — an observed value was 16.0.
Softmax over all classes
Tier 2 softmaxes across all 10,000 classes and then takes the best mapped one. Restricting before the softmax would renormalise a squirrel into a confident bird. As written, a non-bird leaves every bird class low and falls through the threshold — which is the intended behaviour.
Frozen naming
The label map is frozen at ~2023 iNaturalist taxonomy: Downy Woodpecker is Picoides pubescens there and Dryobates pubescens today. CURRENT_NAMES in build_taxonomy.py records renames so the CSV shows today's name while the row stays at the index the model emits. Separately, Wikipedia prefers IOC names — left alone it renames European Starling to Common Starling across the app; the curated names win where they overlap.
python scripts/fetch_models.py      # ~3.5 MB, sha256-pinned. Not committed.
python scripts/build_taxonomy.py    # regenerate taxonomy.csv from the label map
python scripts/validate_tier1.py    # measure real accuracy — run after ANY model change

13 · The notification subsystem Engineer

One NotificationService, four channels, fire-and-forget.

# sightings/controller.py — the response does not wait on this
asyncio.create_task(notification_service.dispatch(sighting.id, device.id))

dispatch opens its own session, so the request's session lifecycle is irrelevant, and wraps everything in a bare except: a notification failure must never surface as a failed upload.

Dispatch order

  1. Load sighting, species, device; count prior sightings of this species at this device.
  2. Collect recipients: device owner ∪ device_users members, deduped.
  3. Load all preferences in one query; missing rows mean defaults.
  4. Load all push subscriptions in one query, before any sending.
  5. Per recipient: apply new-species-only, then the per-(user, device) throttle, then build the channel coroutines they've opted into.
  6. asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) — one dead channel cannot take down the others.
  7. Prune endpoints the push service reported permanently gone.
Why subscriptions load before sending Loading them lazily inside the per-recipient coroutines would have several of them using the same AsyncSession concurrently, which SQLAlchemy does not support. It is not an optimisation.
The monotonic-clock bug, preserved as a lesson The throttle map defaulted a never-notified recipient's last-send to 0.0, which reads as "throttled until time.monotonic() >= interval". On Linux time.monotonic() counts from boot — so for the first 60 seconds of uptime, every first notification was silently suppressed. That dropped the first sighting after any reboot and made CI red on freshly-booted runners. The fix is three lines; finding it was not.

Channel implementations

email_sender.py
SendGrid. HTML body with the image inline via cid:.
sms_sender.py
Twilio. One line, plus the Wikipedia URL when known.
push_sender.py
RFC 8291 aes128gcm payload encryption + RFC 8292 VAPID, on cryptography + aiohttp. Not pywebpush, which is synchronous and would need a thread per send.
wikipedia.py
Three-step chain: REST summary API → web search → constructed URL verified by a 200. A failure is logged, leaves the column null, and is retried on the next sighting of that species.

14 · Simulator & demo mode Engineer

14.1 · The simulator

backend/simulator.py is a virtual feeder that imports and drives the real Pi client — raspberry_pi_code.api_client.BackendClient, unmodified. There is therefore no second upload implementation that can drift from the hardware's.

# backfill 120 sightings across 14 days, then exit
python -m backend.simulator --mode burst --count 120 --days 14

# drip one visit every ~8s until Ctrl-C
python -m backend.simulator --mode live --interval 8

With no --device-token it signs in as the demo owner and reads tokens off GET /devices, so a seeded stack needs zero configuration. Species come from feeder_species.csv; visits are dawn/dusk weighted; confidence is drawn from a per-tier band; placeholder JPEGs are generated at run time from each species' palette (needs Pillow, which is in requirements-dev.txt — the API container never imports it). Burst mode marks uploads delayed=True, which is what the offline-sync path really sends.

14.2 · Demo mode

DEMO_MODE=1 makes an instance safe to hand out.

BehaviourDetail
Boot seedSeeds the demo dataset if the database is empty. Never twice. A failure logs and boots anyway — a demo seed is a convenience, not a precondition for serving. Schema still belongs to Alembic.
Read-onlyEvery user-authenticated write returns 403 with the standard envelope.
Still livePOST /sightings, POST /classify, the heartbeat and POST /login keep working. That's what lets the simulator keep the feed moving.
DiscoveryGET /meta reports demo_mode and — only in demo mode — the published demo login, so the frontend can show a banner and a one-click sign-in.
The allowlist is the entire security surface The check runs as ASGI middleware, before any guard has resolved who is calling, so it decides on method and path alone. Four regexes in backend/demo.py: 
^/login/?$                    # unauthenticated by design
^/sightings/?$                # device_guard — Pi upload
^/classify/?$                 # device_guard — Tier 3 relay
^/devices/\d+/heartbeat/?$    # device_guard — telemetry
Adding a device-facing route means adding it here too.

POST/DELETE /push/subscriptions are deliberately not allowlisted: every demo visitor shares one account, so one stored subscription would push every later sighting to all the other visitors' browsers.

15 · PWA, offline & web push Engineer

# the service worker only registers in a production build — this is how
# the install prompt, offline reload and push are exercised locally
cd frontend && npm run build && npm run preview   # :4173, /api proxied

python scripts/generate_vapid_keys.py    # push keypair → .env
python scripts/generate_pwa_icons.py     # re-render icons (needs Pillow)

15.1 · The service worker

Hand-written (frontend/public/sw.js) rather than plugin-generated, because three different caching strategies are needed and a generator gives one:

App shell
Network-first — so a deploy is actually picked up.
Hashed assets
Cache-first — content-addressed, so they cannot go stale.
API reads
Network-first with cache fallback.

It never caches a non-GET or a non-200, so a 401 cannot outlive the session. It does not call skipWaiting — a new worker takes over on the next visit rather than swapping caches out from under a running page. Registration is production-only: a worker in front of the Vite dev server serves stale modules and fights HMR.

15.2 · Offline reads

The last successful set of API payloads is kept in localStorage and re-mapped on open, so the app paints content on the first render rather than a spinner. The raw payloads are stored, and loadAll was split into fetchRaw + mapAll — a JSON round trip would hand the pages datetime as a string, and a second mapper would drift from the first.

Why the banner needs navigator.onLine too With the worker installed, an offline load succeeds — it is answered from cache — so nothing in the data layer knows anything is wrong. The stale flag alone would never fire.

Writes stay online-only. This is a read cache, not a sync queue.

15.3 · Web push

Key derivation
The VAPID public key is derived from the private key, never read from VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY (which is only cross-checked). A mismatched pair would fail only at delivery time, on every send.
Key stability
Browsers bake the public key into their subscription. Rotating it silently invalidates every existing subscription.
Payload
Carries display text, not ids — the worker has no session and cannot call the API. tag is per-device so a phone that missed several alerts collapses them to the latest per feeder.
Pruning
404/410 from the push service deletes the row; 429/500 leaves it.
Disabled cleanly
With no private key, GET /push/config reports enabled:false, subscriptions are still accepted, nothing is sent, and the web app hides the opt-in.

15.4 · Mobile polish worth noting

Pull-to-refresh is implemented, not inherited: the browser's own gesture reloads the document and throws away the React tree for what is only a data refresh, so overscroll-behavior-y: contain suppresses it and Offline.jsx provides the gesture. 44 px touch targets and 16 px inputs apply under pointer: coarse only, so the desktop layout does not loosen. Lighthouse mobile scores accessibility 100 / best practices 100; the two remaining failures are deliberate (is-crawlable — a private dashboard should not be indexed — and llms-txt, not applicable).

16 · Security model Engineer

ControlBehaviour
Invite is owner-onlyPOST /users had no guard and role was client-supplied — anyone could mint an owner account and enumerate every user's email and phone. Now owner-only with a validated role.
Login throttlingPer account and per client IP: 5 failures / 5 min → 429 + Retry-After. Per-account alone lets one attacker spray many accounts; per-IP alone lets a distributed attempt through.
No account enumerationUnknown email and wrong password return an identical response.
CORSExplicit origin allowlist. * is rejected because credentials are allowed — wildcard plus credentials lets any site drive the API as the logged-in user.
Upload capMAX_UPLOAD_BYTES, 15 MB default. Images are buffered into bytea, so an unbounded body is a memory-exhaustion vector.
Production boot checkWith ENVIRONMENT=production the app refuses to start on a default or <32-char JWT_SECRET, or wildcard CORS. Failing loudly at boot beats discovering it later.
Token separationSeparate guards. A device token is not accepted on user routes, and vice versa.
Passwordsbcrypt only, never plain text.
Images behind authGET /sightings/{id}/image requires a user JWT and 401s without one — verified byte-for-byte on hardware.
SecretsEnv vars only. .env, backups/ and *.dump are gitignored — dumps contain real user records and photographs.
Read the audit output, not the tick pip-audit and npm audit run in CI on every push but are continue-on-error — a transitive CVE with no available fix shouldn't block unrelated work. That means a green CI badge does not mean a clean audit. Open the job.
Threat model, stated honestly This is a LAN-only household application. It defends against a curious guest on your WiFi, an accidental exposure, and its own worst defaults. It has not been designed or reviewed for direct internet exposure, and §3 of the PRD lists internet-accessible deployment as an explicit non-goal.

17 · Testing & CI Engineer

# unit — throwaway SQLite, no services needed
pytest -q                              # 269 passed, 1 skipped

# integration + contract — spins up postgres:16, runs, tears down
bash scripts/run_integration.sh

# frontend
cd frontend && npm test               # 129 passed in 14 files
SuiteTestsWhat only it can prove
backend/tests/211 fnsController and operation behaviour, fast, on SQLite via aiosqlite.
raspberry_pi_code/tests/22Tier-chain logic, offline queue, Tier 3 timeout — with no Pi present.
integration_tests/22Real Postgres: bytea round-trip, real bcrypt login, device-scoped reads, aggregate queries, and model/migration drift.
frontend/src/*.test.*129Mapping, formatters, auth branches, chart rendering, service-worker registration, offline snapshot behaviour.

The contract tests are the interesting ones

They drive the real Pi aiohttp clients against live in-process uvicorn servers — nothing mocked on the wire. Only the GPU itself is stubbed, so the inference contract runs on any machine. They cover the happy path, offline-sync delayed=True, a bad device token, and the 503 model-unavailable fallthrough. test_contract_simulator.py runs the simulator's real CLI against a live server on real Postgres and asserts what landed: image bytes in bytea, per-tier confidence bounds, delayed on backfill, and that the simulator keeps posting while demo mode blocks user writes.

CI

Four jobs on every push and PR to main (.github/workflows/ci.yml): backend (Python 3.11 + 3.12 matrix), integration (a postgres:16 service container), audit (pip-audit + npm audit, non-blocking), and frontend (test then build). Branch protection on main is a recommended manual repo setting — see CONTRIBUTING.md.

A landmine that was found the hard way, twice docker-compose.test.yml once shared the default compose project and the service name db with docker-compose.yml, so run_integration.sh recreated the developer's running dev database container as the test one and then deleted it on exit. The dev data survived only because pg_data is declared in the other file and so was out of that project's reach. The test stack now declares its own project name.

18 · Operating the stack Engineer

18.1 · Health & readiness

EndpointPurposeChecks
GET /healthLivenessNothing. Deliberately dependency-free — a liveness probe that fails on a transient DB blip would have the orchestrator restart a perfectly healthy container.
GET /readyReadinessDatabase reachable and schema migrated to a revision this build knows. 503 when not.
GET /metaIdentityNothing. Public: reports demo_mode + environment so the web app can render the demo banner before login.

The compose healthcheck targets /ready, so docker compose ps only reports healthy once the container can actually serve. Use /health for liveness probes and /ready for load-balancer membership.

18.2 · Migrations

bash scripts/migrate.sh                 # upgrade to head
bash scripts/migrate.sh current         # what revision is this DB on?
bash scripts/migrate.sh check           # fail if models drifted
bash scripts/migrate.sh revision --autogenerate -m "add foo"

The API container runs alembic upgrade head before uvicorn starts, so docker compose up is always migrated.

Upgrading a database that predates Alembic Stamp it, don't upgrade it — otherwise the baseline migration replays over live tables: bash scripts/migrate.sh stamp head.

18.3 · Backup & restore

bash scripts/backup.sh                    # → backups/peck_deck_<UTC>.dump
bash scripts/restore.sh <dump>            # DESTRUCTIVE; prompts
bash scripts/restore.sh <dump> scratch_db # restore elsewhere (no prompt)
bash scripts/backup_smoke_test.sh         # prove a dump actually restores

Because images are bytea, the database dump is the media backup — there is no image directory to copy separately. Uses pg_dump -Fc: compressed, and required by pg_restore. Plain SQL balloons on bytea because images get hex-escaped. Everything runs inside the db container, so no local Postgres client is needed.

Why the smoke test hashes the image bytes It restores into a throwaway database and compares row counts and a SHA-256 of the concatenated image bytes. That digest is the entire point: a backup that restored every row but truncated bytea would lose every photograph, and a row count alone would never catch it.

18.4 · Logging

Structured, with a request id bound per request and threaded into every log line. Sighting creation logs the tier used; Tier 3 classification logs its result; notification outcomes are logged per channel. Grep a request_id from an error envelope to get the whole request's story.

19 · Hardware build guide Engineer Owner

Status — this is the one open phase Every claim below is tagged. Bench-verified means it has been run on the actual Pi. Specified means it is a researched recommendation that nobody has built yet. Do not read this section as a report of a working outdoor installation; read it as the plan for one.

19.1 · What is proven, and what isn't

ItemStatusEvidence
Camera capture (IMX708)Verified~300 KB JPEG at 1920×1080 in ~1.0 s, real sensor, via project code.
Tier 1 on-device inferenceVerified57.9 ms avg, 12 ms load, 20/20 on the curated set.
Tier 2 GPU serverVerifiedtorch 2.11.0+cu128, sm_120. ~29 ms local, ~1 s from the Pi over WiFi.
Tier chain handoff on hardwareVerifiedLive capture → T1 → T2 → T3 → best-effort retained, across a real LAN hop.
GPIO backend (C0–C2)Verifiedrpi-lgpio shim on RP1; output toggle and both internal pulls correct.
Trigger code path (C3 loopback)Verified9/9. BCM27 → BCM17 through a breadboard, edges driven by pinctrl from outside the process under test.
Backend + Postgres uploadVerifiedReal multipart POST → 300,518-byte JPEG in bytea; byte-identical on retrieval; 401 without a JWT.
Real trigger sensor (C4)OpenNothing is wired to the header. C3 proves the code, not the sensor.
Tier 3 on hardwareOpenReached the backend, got a clean 503 — no API key set. See Appendix C.
Full field testOpenNo real bird has ever completed the loop.
Enclosure, power, mountingSpecifiedResearched in OUTDOOR_DEPLOYMENT.md. Not built.

19.2 · Power — the binding constraint

A Pi 5 draws ~3.0 W headless, ~3.7 W with the camera streaming, up to 8.8 W loaded. Call it 4.0 W working average with inference bursts and uploads. That number decides everything else.

A Ring battery pack cannot run a Pi 5 Not "runs it briefly" — it physically cannot. Capacity: 22 Wh against a 4 W load is under five hours. No output port: the micro-USB is a charge input; discharge is via proprietary spring contacts. Current ceiling: a Pi 5 wants 5 V @ 5 A, which at the pack's 3.65 V nominal is over 7 A on the input side — a protection circuit built for a ~1 A camera load will trip or sag, and you cannot boost your way out of a cell that will not source the current. The thing worth keeping from the idea is the ergonomics — a sealed, swappable, tool-free block — not the pack.

Cold matters more than most people expect: standard Li-ion must not be charged below freezing, which is most of a Spokane winter. LiFePO4 (rung C) handles cold far better, and a BMS with a low-temperature charge cutoff is not optional if a panel is involved.

19.3 · Triggering — the shipped default is wrong

PIR does not detect birds config.py defaults to TRIGGER_TYPE=pir. Change it. Feathers are outstanding thermal insulation — a bird's core is 104–107 °F but its surface, which is all a PIR sees, is close to ambient. Worse, consumer PIR modules advertise "no false alarms from birds and small animals" as a feature; you would be fighting the sensor's designed behaviour. And it degrades in summer as ambient rises toward the bird's apparent surface temperature.
RankTriggerReliabilityCostWorks with the existing code?
1Perch microswitchExcellent~$5Yes — falling edge, pull-up. Wire it as ir_beam.
2Modulated IR beam (38 kHz)Good~$10Yes — that is what the ir_beam class is.
3Camera motion detectionGood$0No — new code, and burns power continuously.
4Microwave doppler (RCWL-0516)Poor~$3Triggers on branches, rain, and passing cars.
5PIRPoor for birds~$3Yes, but see above.

Why it wins: immune to sun angle, smoke, snow and ambient temperature; zero standby current, unlike an IR emitter; and it self-selects for the shot you want — the bird is at a known position, so focus distance and framing are known, which is a large free accuracy win for Tier 1. The trade-off, stated plainly: you only catch birds that land on the perch. Hovering birds and ground feeders are invisible. Decide on that consciously.

If you use a beam instead, one piece of advice dominates: use a modulated 38 kHz receiver (TSSP4038 / TSOP4838), not a bare photodiode. The sun is a massive broadband IR source and Spokane's winter noon sun sits ~19° above the horizon — it will find your receiver and blind it. Mount emitter and receiver on one rigid bracket, or a 33 °F daily swing will misalign them.

A guard that doesn't exist yet Snow, a leaf, a spider web or ash can block a beam persistently — which looks like one trigger then silence, or a trigger storm. There is no stuck-beam fault check in IRBeamTrigger today, and this is the sensor's main outdoor failure mode. Also watch flocking: starlings occupying a perch at a 30 s debounce is 120 captures/hour, filling MAX_QUEUED_SIGHTINGS (200) in under two hours if the network is down.

19.4 · Thermal & enclosure

The Pi already throttles on a bench The hardware inventory records 73.6 °C idle with throttled=0x80000 — the soft temperature limit had already been hit — in open air, in a climate-controlled room. A sealed box in a Spokane July (record high 109 °F) is a thermal failure, not a thermal risk. A later session measured 59.3 °C idle / 64.2 °C under load, so cooling changes between sessions mattered a great deal — which is exactly why item 5 below is worth building.

Ranked by effect per dollar: light-coloured enclosure; a conduction path from the Pi's heatsink to the enclosure wall (aluminium plate + thermal pad); a sun shield with an air gap; and only then active airflow. And, separately from heat:

Condensation is the hazard with no off-season Spokane gets ~16 inches of rain a year but a ~33 °F day-to-night swing every day of the year. Design for the swing and the rain takes care of itself. That means a pressure-equalisation vent (Gore PolyVent or equivalent — do not skip it), colour-indicating silica gel you rotate, and glands matched to the actual cable diameter.
HazardJanFebMarAprMayJunJulAugSepOctNovDec
Freeze
Snow
Heat
Smoke
Condensation
Bird traffic

High hazard Moderate Low Peak bird traffic Spokane, WA (47.6 °N)

Read the bottom row against the rest. Feeder traffic peaks Nov–Mar — precisely when the power budget is worst (8–9 h daylight, cold-derated batteries) and condensation is worst. Plan the real deployment for winter and the shakedown for fall.

19.5 · Software changes the outdoor build implies

#ChangeWhereWhy
1Default TRIGGER_TYPE to ir_beamraspberry_pi_code/config.pyPIR doesn't detect birds.
2Lock autofocus + set a shutter floorcamera/pi_camera.pyThere is no AF configuration at all today; the lens hunts.
3Stuck-beam / stuck-switch fault detectionraspberry_pi_code/trigger/Snow or debris = permanent trigger or trigger storm.
4Dawn/dusk scheduling + POWER_OFF_ON_HALT=1new systemd timer~2× runtime for no hardware cost.
5Report SoC temp + throttle flags in the heartbeatPi → POST /devices/{id}/heartbeatYou cannot debug thermal problems you cannot see.
6Report battery voltage/percentage in the heartbeatsame"When do I swap the pack" should be a dashboard answer.
7Enable the hardware watchdog/boot/firmware/config.txtAn unattended outdoor Pi must self-recover from a hang.
8Logs to tmpfs; consider USB SSD bootOS levelSD corruption is the classic long-term killer.
9Adaptive debounce for flocking speciespipeline.pyNice-to-have, after the field trial.

Items 5 and 6 are the highest-leverage on the list: the Devices page already exists. Surfacing temperature, throttle state and battery there turns every remaining question in this section from speculation into telemetry, on a path that is already built and tested.

19.6 · Staged bring-up

Do not go from bench to backyard in one step. Each stage changes exactly one variable, so a failure is diagnosable.

19.7 · Open questions the docs can't answer

  1. Is "no external power at the feeder" still a requirement, or an inherited assumption? It is the constraint driving the most cost and complexity here. If an eave with mains is acceptable long-term, most of this section's difficulty evaporates. Worth an explicit decision either way.
  2. Pole or eave as the permanent home? Opposite strengths; the answer changes the battery, network and baffle spend.
  3. Perch switch or IR beam? Cheaper and more reliable versus catching ground feeders and hovering birds.
  4. How often are you willing to walk out there? Every power decision reduces to this number.
  5. What is the real accuracy on wild birds? Unknown until Stage 1. If it comes back at 70%, that is a bigger problem than any enclosure question and it reorders this entire list.

20 · Contributing Engineer

20.1 · Clone to green in five minutes

git clone https://github.com/dnorris823/Peck_Deck.git && cd Peck_Deck
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r backend/requirements-dev.txt -r raspberry_pi_code/requirements.txt

Then docker compose up --build and python -m backend.simulator --mode burst --count 120 --days 14 to get a populated stack to look at.

20.2 · Where to start reading

20.3 · Conventions that are not negotiable

Async everywhere
All DB and network I/O. A sync call in a handler blocks the loop.
Litestar, not FastAPI
In backend/. The inference server is the FastAPI one.
bcrypt always
Never store a plain-text password.
Images as bytea
Not on disk. Served through the authenticated route.
Alembic owns the schema
No create_all() in app code. Model change → migration.
Pi code stays self-contained
raspberry_pi_code/ imports nothing from backend/.
Secrets in env vars
Never committed.
Regenerate the OpenAPI snapshot
After any route change, so the contract diff is reviewable.

20.4 · Branch & PR flow

main should always be green. Short-lived feature branch → PR into main, one logical change per PR where practical, CI green before merge. Branch protection is a one-time manual toggle in repo Settings, documented in CONTRIBUTING.md.

20.5 · Project status

Good first contributions Items 1, 2 and 3 from §19.5 are self-contained, well-specified, and unblock the field test. Item 5 (temperature in the heartbeat) touches the Pi, the API, and the Devices page, which makes it an excellent tour of the whole stack in one small PR. Fixing the two entries in Appendix C is smaller still.

TRIGGER_GPIO_PIN17BCM numbering. Header pin 11.
DEBOUNCE_SECONDS30Minimum spacing between captures.
IMAGE_WIDTH / _HEIGHT / JPEG_QUALITY1920/1080/90~300 KB per frame.
CACHE_DIR/var/lib/peck_deck/cacheMust be writable by the service user.
MAX_CACHE_IMAGES25Bounds unqueued images only.
MAX_QUEUED_SIGHTINGS200Bounds the backlog. This is the real limit during an outage.
TIER2_REQUEST_TIMEOUT30Seconds.
TIER3_REQUEST_TIMEOUT25Kept below DEBOUNCE_SECONDS so an unreachable backend cannot stall past the next trigger.
SYNC_INTERVAL_SECONDS60Offline-queue drain attempt interval.
MODEL_PATH / TAXONOMY_PATHrepo-relativeOverride only if assets live elsewhere.

Appendix C · Known rough edges

Things that are true of the repository as of this revision and that would otherwise cost a newcomer an afternoon.

1 · The Tier 3 key is documented under the wrong name .env.example line 72 suggests CLAUDE_API_KEY. The code reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (backend/config.py:84). Setting the documented name does nothing and POST /classify keeps returning 503 — which is very likely why Tier 3 was recorded as unreachable during hardware bring-up. FLEDGE_ROADMAP.md repeats the wrong name in two places. Fix: correct .env.example and the roadmap.
2 · A duplicate key in the Vite config frontend/vite.config.js declares preview twice. The second declaration (port + proxy) wins, so the first one's allowedHosts: ['.ts.net', …] is silently discarded — which would surface as a blocked-host error when previewing over a Tailscale name. Fix: merge them into one object.
3 · No autofocus configuration exists camera/pi_camera.py never touches the lens. Outdoors this means the lens hunts between frames and can settle on the feeder body or the background rather than the bird. This is §19.5 item 2 and it is the single most likely software cause of a disappointing field-accuracy number.
4 · Two checkouts exist on the Pi ~/coding/Peck_Deck is the live one — it has the Python 3.11 .venv with tflite-runtime. ~/peck_deck/Peck_Deck is an abandoned copy stuck at an early commit. Also: do not install numpy ≥2 into that venv — it breaks picamera2's simplejpeg C extension, which is compiled against the system numpy 1.24.2.
5 · Placeholders that look like features Misidentified? on the sighting detail, Play 7s clip, Download, and per-station recipient lists are visible but not wired. Video capture is designed for — video_data exists on the model — and deliberately deferred.

Appendix D · Glossary

bytea
PostgreSQL's binary column type. Where every sighting photograph lives.
Debounce
Ignoring repeat triggers within a window, so one visit is one sighting. Two layers: bouncetime=200 ms in the GPIO handler, and DEBOUNCE_SECONDS (30 s) in the pipeline.
Delayed sighting
One uploaded from the offline queue after connectivity returned. Flagged in the database and mentioned in the notification.
Device token
A feeder's long-lived credential. Not a user JWT and not accepted on user routes.
FLEDGE
The project's phased roadmap — everything buildable without the Pi or the GPU on the bench, so progress could ship from anywhere.
Projection
Mapping Tier 2's 10,000 iNat21 classes onto the shared 965-row taxonomy by scientific name. 869 map.
PWA
Progressive Web App — the web app installed to a home screen, with offline reads and push, and no app store.
RP1
The Pi 5's I/O controller. Why RPi.GPIO must resolve to the rpi-lgpio shim.
Station
The app's word for a registered feeder. A Device row.
Taxonomy
taxonomy.csv — 965 rows whose order is the model's output index contract. Generated, never hand-edited.
Tier
One of the three identifiers: 1 local on the Pi, 2 LAN GPU, 3 Claude API.
VAPID
RFC 8292. The keypair identifying this server to browser push services. Rotating it invalidates every existing subscription.
